paras: The threatened lynching of Frank Johnson and Enoch Echols was an attempt in April 1882 by armed white men from counties around Athens, Georgia, to take two young Black prisoners from the Athens jail and lynch them for the shooting of a University student, Walter Rountree. According to the Athens Banner, an advance guard of about 150 men was met outside town by a committee of citizens and went home without reaching the jail. The two men were later convicted of assault with intent to murder after a post-mortem traced the fatal bullet to the pistol of Rountree's own brother.

On the evening of April 4, 1882, Walter Rountree, a student from Quitman, was shot in Athens and died the next day; Johnson and Echols were arrested at Miles Johnson's shop and jailed. The Banner Watchman traced the shooting to weeks of friction over the sidewalk and said Johnson fired the fatal shot. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of willful and premeditated murder against Johnson, with Echols as abettor.

That night, an Augusta dispatch said, about 300 armed Black men surrounded the jail but made no attempt to release the prisoners. The mayor detailed fifty citizens to guard the jail and summoned the 'ringleaders' to court, though Mayor Rucker soon telegraphed that reports of excitement were greatly exaggerated.

Several days before April 25, by the Banner's account, the Athens authorities learned that men from adjacent counties planned to lynch the prisoners on a set Thursday night. The plan was kept quiet, extra police were posted in the city, and the regular force of seven men under Chief Davis, armed with Winchesters and pistols, guarded the jail from its roof. When the guards entered the jail around midnight, the prisoners took them for a mob and expressed great fear until they learned who they were.

Meanwhile a delegation of citizens rode out and met the advance guard near the paper mill: about 150 men carrying breech-loading shotguns, who said 600 more were coming behind. The committee asked that the law take its course, and the men answered that they had not come to override the town's wishes and would disperse. They added that they would march several thousand strong into the city if needed, and then returned home.

On a student's statement, a medical commission exhumed Rountree's body and found that the fatal ball matched the pistol of his brother Bartow, not Johnson's. The charge was reduced to assault with intent to murder, and at trial the student J. W. Twiggs testified that Walter Rountree had stopped the two men, cursed Johnson and kicked him before the shooting began. On May 18 the jury found both men guilty, and Judge Erwin sentenced each to ten years in the penitentiary, with an appeal expected. A Savannah dispatch reported the city quiet, with no demonstrations from whites or Black residents.

The lynching party appears only in a Banner report reprinted by the Savannah Morning News on April 25, which praised the would-be lynchers as 'the best men' of their sections and 'quiet, determined citizens' while urging that the law take its course. Early wire coverage in Savannah, Richmond and New York called the shooting murder, the Richmond Dispatch blaming 'Colored Roughs' and the Savannah paper headlining 'The Assassins in Jail' and 'A Colored Mob in the Streets.' A Macon letter spoke of the 'assassination of young Rountree' and blamed 'Radical negroes' for racial antagonism.

Once the post-mortem was known, the Savannah paper reported the charge 'Modified,' and the Abbeville Press and Banner headlined that a white man trying to kill a Black man had shot his own brother. No Black-press account of the episode was found.

Early Athens accounts said Johnson fired the fatal shot after pursuing the students, while the later post-mortem and sworn trial testimony placed the fatal ball in Bartow Rountree's pistol and had Walter Rountree acting first.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Johnson and Enoch Echols
bases: An armed party from adjacent counties came to Athens to lynch two Black prisoners held for the shooting of a white student, and dispersed without reaching the jail (A7).

No one was killed: the advance guard of about 150 armed men who came to lynch the prisoners turned back after meeting a citizens' committee, and the two men were later tried and sentenced (A7, A9). It is a threatened lynching only.
The lynching party is reported only in the Athens Banner as quoted by the Savannah Morning News (A7); the shooting, arrests and trial are corroborated by several papers (A3, A8, A9, A10, A11).

accounts.label: Athens Banner (town's account of the lynching party)
accounts.gist: Men from adjacent counties set a Thursday night to lynch the prisoners; a citizens' committee met their 150-man advance guard near the paper mill and persuaded them to go home while police guarded the jail.

accounts.label: Banner Watchman (early account of the shooting)
accounts.gist: Johnson and Echols pursued the students after earlier friction and Johnson fired the fatal shot.

accounts.label: Post-mortem and trial testimony
accounts.gist: The fatal ball matched Bartow Rountree's pistol; Twiggs testified that Walter Rountree kicked and cursed Johnson before the shooting.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'MURDER IN ATHENS' and 'The Assassins in Jail-A Colored Mob in the Streets', casting armed Black residents as the threat.
The Athens Banner opposed the lynching but called the party 'the best men' and 'quiet, determined citizens' come 'to the redress of a great wrong'.
Later reports headlined that the charge against the negroes was 'Modified' and that a white man 'Shoots His own Brother to Death'.
Richmond and New York papers ran the Augusta wire of the shooting, the Dispatch calling the accused 'Colored Roughs'.

versions.value: Bartow Rountree, the victim's brother (post-mortem; trial testimony)

conflicts.note: The later post-mortem and sworn testimony are better evidence than the early Banner Watchman account; the charge was reduced accordingly.
